title: Given a Scenario, Configure Appropriate Resources to Achieve Observability

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud environments can contain many virtual machines, containers, applications, databases, network components, and cloud services.
When something goes wrong, administrators need enough information to understand what happened and where the problem occurred. That is the purpose of observability.
CompTIA wants you to recognize logging, tracing, monitoring, and alerting.
sections.callout: Logs tell you what happened → metrics show how the system is behaving → traces show how activity moved through the system → alerts identify conditions that need attention.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Does the administrator need to collect events, measure performance, follow activity through multiple services, or respond to a detected problem?
sections.callout: Events → logs. Numbers → metrics. Request path → tracing. Something needs attention → alerting.

sections.title: Logging
paragraphs: Logging records events generated by applications, operating systems, cloud services, security controls, and infrastructure.
Logs can contain authentication events, errors, application activity, configuration changes, network events, security events, and service activity.
Think: What happened? Logs provide recorded evidence of previous activity.
sections.callout: If you need recorded events from a cloud resource → think logging.

entries.title: Collection
paragraphs: Collection gathers logs from the systems and services producing them, including virtual machines, containers, applications, databases, firewalls, cloud APIs, and identity systems.
Think: First, get the logs.
entries.recognitionCue: Gather log records from resources → collection.

entries.title: Aggregation
paragraphs: Aggregation brings logs from multiple sources together in a central location.
Instead of checking many systems individually, administrators can search one centralized log platform.
Think: Many logs → one place.
entries.recognitionCue: Centralize logs from multiple systems → aggregation.

entries.title: Retention
paragraphs: Retention determines how long logs remain stored.
The required period can depend on troubleshooting, investigations, business or compliance requirements, and storage cost.
Deleting logs too quickly can remove needed evidence; keeping every log forever can increase cost unnecessarily.
Think: How long do we need to keep the evidence?
entries.recognitionCue: Determine how long logs remain available → retention.

sections.title: Tracing
paragraphs: Tracing follows an individual request or transaction as it moves through components of an application.
It is especially useful with microservices, distributed applications, APIs, and multiple cloud services.
If a customer request travels through a web application, authentication service, inventory service, payment service, and database, tracing can identify where the path failed or slowed.
Think: Follow the request.
sections.callout: If one transaction must be tracked through multiple services → think tracing.

sections.title: Monitoring
paragraphs: Monitoring continuously observes the health, availability, and performance of cloud resources.
Administrators may monitor CPU, memory, storage, network traffic, request rates, response times, error rates, and availability.
Think: How is the environment behaving right now?
sections.callout: If the goal is to continuously observe cloud health or performance → think monitoring.

entries.title: Metrics
paragraphs: A metric is a measurable numerical value describing system behavior or performance.
Examples include CPU percentage, memory usage, response time, requests per second, storage utilization, and error rate.
Think: Give me the numbers.
entries.recognitionCue: Numeric measurement of cloud performance or condition → metric.

sections.title: Alerting
paragraphs: Alerting notifies administrators or automated systems when a defined condition requires attention.
An alert may be triggered by high CPU, low storage capacity, increased error rates, an unavailable service, or suspicious activity.
Think: Something crossed the line—tell somebody.
sections.callout: If a condition requires a notification → think alerting.

entries.title: Triage
paragraphs: Triage determines the importance and priority of an alert.
Administrators decide whether it is legitimate, how severe it is, which systems are affected, and whether immediate action is required.
Think: How serious is this alert?
entries.recognitionCue: Evaluate and prioritize an alert → triage.

entries.title: Response
paragraphs: Response is the action taken after an alert has been evaluated.
Actions can include investigating logs, restarting a service, scaling resources, blocking malicious activity, escalating to another team, or opening an incident ticket.
Think: We know what the alert means. Now act.
entries.recognitionCue: Take action after evaluating an alert → response.

sections.title: Putting Observability Together
paragraphs: Suppose users report that a cloud application is slow. Monitoring shows high response time. Metrics show CPU utilization at 95%. Logs show repeated application errors. Tracing shows requests slowing at the database service.
Alerting notifies the operations team, triage determines that production customers are affected, and response drives investigation and correction.
That is observability working as a system.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Decide how long logs remain → Retention
Follow a request across services → Tracing
Notify when a condition is reached → Alerting
Determine alert severity or priority → Triage

entries.title: Logs vs. Metrics
paragraphs: Logs are individual recorded events. Metrics are numerical measurements.
'Application produced error 500 at 13:05' is a log. 'Error rate reached 4%' is a metric.

entries.title: Logging vs. Tracing
paragraphs: Logging shows what individual systems recorded. Tracing shows how one request moved through multiple systems.

entries.title: Monitoring vs. Alerting
paragraphs: Monitoring observes conditions. Alerting notifies when a condition requires attention. Monitoring can occur without an alert.

entries.title: Collection vs. Aggregation
paragraphs: Collection gathers logs. Aggregation centralizes logs from many sources.

entries.title: Triage vs. Response
paragraphs: Triage determines seriousness. Response takes action.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: How long do we keep them? → Retention
Tell me something is wrong → Alerting
How serious is the alert? → Triage
